extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political science, journalists, and general readers interested in public opinion and the media
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of how individuals and publics form opinions about public affairs, focusing on the limits of access to facts, the role of pseudo-environments, censorship/propaganda, and the institutional requirements for informed democratic decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior based on pseudo-environment (pictures inside the head)
rubrics_metrics.description: What each man does is based not on direct and certain knowledge, but on pictures made by himself or given to him; the way in which the world is imagined determines at any particular moment what men will do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: if a map says the world is flat a sailor avoids the edge; if someone finds yellow dirt that looks like gold he will behave as if he found gold. Propaganda and the formation of class consciousness are efforts to alter these pictures. The pseudo-environment governs effort, feelings, hopes rather than actual accomplishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors limiting access to facts
rubrics_metrics.description: There are chief factors which limit people's access to the facts: artificial censorships, limitations of social contact, the comparatively meager time available each day for paying attention to public affairs, distortion from compressing events into very short messages, difficulty of making a small vocabulary express a complicated world, and fear of facing facts that threaten routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These external limitations are the starting point for explaining why public opinion often misrepresents the real environment; they should be used as categories for assessing why a public lacks accurate information about an issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stored images, preconceptions, and prejudices interpret incoming messages
rubrics_metrics.description: The trickle of messages from the outside is affected by stored-up images, preconceptions, and prejudices which interpret, fill them out, and in turn direct attention and vision itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating public responses or news coverage, consider how prior stereotypes and preconceptions shape what people notice and how they interpret compressed or partial information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and privacy create the barrier necessary for propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Without some form of censorship, propaganda in the strict sense of the word is impossible. In order to conduct propaganda there must be some barrier between the public and the event; access to the real environment must be limited before anyone can create a pseudo-environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between explicit state/military censorship and socially accepted privacy norms (e.g., diplomatic confidentiality, private corporate meetings) — both function as barriers enabling others to shape public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of control that enable shaping of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who control the selection of correspondents, control their movements, read and censor their messages, operate the wires, and have legal powers over publishers, passports, mails, customs, blockades and secret services can determine what the public perceives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete indicators (who accredits correspondents, censorship practices, control of cables/passports) to evaluate how much a particular authority can shape or manufacture public opinion; military and diplomatic censorship tends to be more complete and consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective reporting and repetition as techniques to produce inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: By emphasizing particular facts (e.g., German 'heavy losses' at Verdun) and omitting others (e.g., French casualties), and by constant repetition and formulaic phrasing, authorities can build a persistent mental picture that leads the public to the desired inferences without explicit argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing news or official communiqués, examine omissions and repetitive motifs; consider how phrasing and repeated statistics function to create impressions rather than to present a balanced factual account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale, organization, and cost required to create a unified public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating a fairly uniform set of ideas for an entire nation requires extensive machinery and resources (example: Creel's wartime operations involved thousands of releases, tens of thousands of speakers, periodicals to teachers, lantern slides, posters, and use of civic institutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence or absence of sustained organizational effort, funding, and distribution channels as a criterion for judging whether a given campaign can realistically reach and shape 'everyone' on a subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure and economic barriers affect circulation of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Means of communication and transport (mails, wires, railways, ports, cables, tariffs, monopolies) substantially influence the supply and quality of information; monopolies and costs can create barriers to exchange of news and opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess physical and economic access (cable control, port/terminal monopolies, travel costs, postal/censorship regimes) to understand differential exposure to information across regions and classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy norms determine what is withheld and affect reliability of public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Notions of what is private (incomes, salaries, directors' meetings, cabinet deliberations, ambassadorial communications, employer-employee contracts) vary over time and place; these private domains limit what facts can be known publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a public opinion or a reported 'fact,' ask how the reporter accessed it: who saw, heard, counted, or named the thing; how much was that person permitted to see; what part of the population was observed. The inability to answer such questions signals distance between public opinion and events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government needs independent expert organizations to interpret unseen facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative government cannot work successfully unless there is an independent, expert organization for making the unseen facts intelligible to decision-makers; personal representation should be supplemented by representation of the unseen facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the existence and quality of expert, nonpartisan institutions (political science, statistical bureaus, independent research organs) as a metric for how well a polity can overcome the defects of decentralized, uninformed public opinion and enable competent decision-making.
